  ## Cozy theme research for the learning app
  
  **1. What makes a UI feel cozy**
  - **Shape and surface:** generous corner radii (16–28px on cards, fully rounded pill buttons), soft diffuse shadows, soft pastel surfaces with dark readable text. Keep the brightest color for the one active element ([Playful Rounded kit](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@wrongstack/core@0.295.1/design-kits/playful-rounded/KIT.md), [daisyUI claymorphism](https://trends.daisyui.com/trend/claymorphism/)).
  - **Low stakes:** cozy games are defined by soft visuals, low risk and easy exits ([Replay journal, 2024](https://czasopisma.uni.lodz.pl/Replay/article/download/24071/24087/59119)). Clutter breaks the calm ([SDLC Corp](https://sdlccorp.com/post/the-art-of-designing-intuitive-user-interfaces-in-cozy-games/)). For this app that means no punitive red states, a "gentle error" color, and failure framed as "try again".
  - **Products to borrow from:** Headspace (rounded shapes, slow easing), Duolingo (chunky progress bar, celebration only at milestones), Linear and Arc (restraint, tinted neutrals, one accent color), Animal Crossing (pill-shaped speech bubbles for chat).
  - **Never pure #000 or #FFF for large areas:** use slightly tinted neutrals.
  - **Motion:** 150–300ms ease-out, nothing that loops, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.
  
  **2. Default palette ("Frost": light blue / white / silver)**
  I calculated these contrast ratios myself with the WCAG formula.
  
  | Token | Hex | Notes |
  |---|---|---|
  | background | `#F4F8FB` | cool off-white |
  | surface (cards, chat bubbles, input) | `#FFFFFF` | |
  | surface-2 / silver | `#E8EEF3` | tabs, hover states |
  | border / silver | `#D3DCE5` | decorative only |
  | primary | `#2F6FAF` | white text on it 5.23:1, passes AA |
  | primary-soft | `#DCEBF7` | selected and highlight fill; text on it 11.9:1 |
  | accent (sky) | `#7FB3E0` | decorative only (2.2:1): XP fill, glows |
  | text | `#1E2A3A` | 13.6:1 on background |
  | muted text | `#5A6B7D` | 5.13:1 on background, 5.48:1 on white |
  | success | `#2E7D5B` | 5.0:1 on white |
  | gentle error | `#B5524A` | 4.92:1 on white |
  
  - Don't use `#3A7BBF` as a button color: it only reaches 4.41:1 and fails AA.
  - Silver tones (`#A9B6C4`, 2.06:1) must never carry text.
  
  **Unlockable theme ideas** (background / surface / primary / accent; check text contrast for each one in code):
  - **Sunset:** `#FFF4EC` / `#FFFFFF` / `#C2553A` / `#F4A261`
  - **Forest:** `#F1F5EE` / `#FBFCF9` / `#3F6B4A` / `#A3C49A`
  - **Sakura:** `#FDF3F5` / `#FFFFFF` / `#B04A6B` / `#F5B8C8`
  - **Parchment / RPG:** `#F5ECD7` / `#FBF5E6` / `#7A4E2D` / `#C9A227`, with a serif display font
  - **Night Sky (dark):** `#141B2D` / `#1E2740` / `#8FB8FF` / `#F2D27A`, text `#E6ECF5`
  - **Matcha:** `#F3F5EC` / `#FFFFFF` / `#55703B` / `#C5D6A0`
  
  **3. Typography**
  - **Recommendation:** **Nunito** for the whole UI. It is rounded, friendly, a variable font, and reads well at chat sizes ([Google Fonts](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Nunito)).
  - **Optional:** **Fraunces** for headings in the Parchment theme ([Google Fonts](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Fraunces)).
  - **Alternative:** offer **Lexend**, which was designed for reading proficiency ([Google Fonts](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Lexend)), as a readability toggle.
  - **Avoid:** Quicksand for body text; it is too thin at small sizes.
  
  **4. Implementation**
  - **Tokens and theme switching:** keep semantic CSS variables in `:root` and override them per theme with `[data-theme="sunset"]{...}`. Map them into Tailwind v4 with `@theme inline { --color-background: var(--background); ... }` so utilities like `bg-primary` follow the active theme ([Tailwind theme docs](https://tailwindcss.com/docs/theme)).
  - **Dark variant:** for Night Sky, add `@custom-variant dark (&:where([data-theme="night"], [data-theme="night"] *));` ([Tailwind dark mode docs](https://tailwindcss.com/docs/dark-mode)).
  - **shadcn/ui:** it already uses exactly these names (`--background`, `--primary`, `--muted-foreground`, `--radius`, and so on) in OKLCH plus `@theme inline` ([shadcn theming docs](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/theming)). Each theme is then just one CSS block. Set `--radius: 1rem` for the cozy look.
  - **Registry for locking and unlocking:** keep one typed array, `THEMES = [{id, name, unlock: {sessions: n}, swatch: [...]}]`. Store the user's unlocked IDs and selected theme in localStorage or the DB, and set `document.documentElement.dataset.theme`.
  - **Locked themes:** show as grayed-out swatches with a padlock and a hint like "Complete 3 sessions".
  - **Adding a theme:** one CSS block plus one array entry.
  - **Avoiding a theme flash:** set `data-theme` in an inline `<head>` script before the page renders.
  
  **Motion libraries**
  - **Motion** (formerly Framer Motion, [motion.dev](https://motion.dev)): use `LazyMotion` with `m` components to keep the bundle small ([bundle-size guide](https://motion.dev/docs/react-reduce-bundle-size)). Good for XP bar springs and layout transitions.
  - **canvas-confetti:** tiny, and its `disableForReducedMotion` option turns confetti off entirely for users who prefer reduced motion ([GitHub](https://github.com/catdad/canvas-confetti)). Use it only for session completion and theme unlocks.
  - **Lottie:** skip it. The player is heavy and needs designed assets.
  
  **5. Gamification without clutter**
  - **XP bar:** a thin (6–8px) rounded bar under the top tabs, accent fill, spring animation on gain, and a small "+20 XP" chip that fades out.
  - **Session progress:** a row of 5–10 dots or a segmented bar rather than percentages.
  - **Boss health bar:** used only in "boss" review rounds. A rounded bar with a cute icon that "shakes" gently (2px, 200ms) on a correct answer; never flash red at the user.
  - **Section map:** a vertical winding path of circular nodes, Duolingo-style, in its own tab rather than in the chat view. Completed nodes are filled primary, the current node has a soft pulsing ring, locked nodes are silver.
  - **Rewards:** a theme unlock gets a toast card ("New theme: Sakura") with a "Try it" button.
  - **Overall rule:** at most one celebratory effect per milestone, and the chat area itself stays clean.

  ## Recommended architecture: a light upfront outline, content generated per unit, and a deterministic learner model
  
  **Core principle:** let code (a small state machine) decide when to advance, remediate or trigger a boss and how hard the next question should be. Let Claude write the questions, explanations and story, grade answers, and check its own content. This keeps adaptivity testable and keeps prompts short. Khan Academy found that long prompts make the model "randomly ignore" instructions, and that putting good context in front of the model before it reasons improved accuracy.
  
  ### 1. Curriculum generation
  - One call to a strong model with a JSON schema returns a **skill graph**: 6–15 concepts, sized to stated time at roughly 5–8 minutes per concept. Each concept has an id, name, learning objective (a Bloom verb such as apply/analyze), prerequisite ids, common misconceptions and "anchor facts". Concepts are grouped into 3–5 sections in prerequisite order, along with the story premise and a final-boss scenario.
  - Evidence: research reports LLMs are workable at finding concepts but **prerequisite edges are less reliable** (arXiv 2504.08856; InstructKG 2602.17111; ACE, JEDM). Mitigation: validate the graph as a DAG in code, and let the user edit or confirm scope in a 10-second "quest map" screen.
  - LearnLM frames pedagogy as instruction-following through system prompts. That fits a system-prompt-driven design. Claude for Education's Learning mode uses Socratic prompting. Neither publishes a curriculum-generation recipe, so this design is my synthesis, not something either documents.
  
  ### 2. Upfront vs. on-demand generation
  - **Upfront:** only the outline and story arc (one call, about 5–15 seconds behind a loading animation). This keeps the story and section boundaries consistent.
  - **On demand (JIT):** each unit (exposition plus a batch of 3–4 questions at the targeted difficulty) is generated when the learner reaches it. **Prefetch the next unit while the user answers the current one**, which hides most of the latency. Regenerate only if mastery moves enough to change the plan.
  - Trade-off: on-demand costs more calls but keeps content adaptive and avoids wasting tokens on content the learner never reaches. Put the stable prefix (system prompt, skill graph, story bible) first and use **prompt caching** to cut cost and latency.
  
  ### 3. Learner model (prototype-sized)
  - For each concept, store an **Elo-style score** θ_c, and give each question a difficulty b from 1 to 5 mapped to an Elo scale. Predicted p = σ(θ_c − b), updated by θ_c += K·(correct − p) with K about 0.4 (decay it over time). This is simpler than BKT and gives difficulty targeting for free. Duolingo's Birdbrain likewise jointly estimates learner ability and item difficulty, but I couldn't confirm that it uses Elo specifically.
  - **Difficulty selection:** pick b so that p ≈ 0.82. The "85% rule" (Wilson et al., 2019) is derived for gradient-descent learners on binary tasks, so treat it as a heuristic, not proven for human concept learning.
  - **Rules:**
    - Mastered = p at difficulty 3 ≥ 0.8 and at least 3 attempts.
    - Two misses in a row, or rolling accuracy below 60% over 4 attempts → insert a remediation unit targeting the misconception that was hit.
    - The first 2 answers correct at difficulty ≥ 4 → offer "skip ahead" to the mini-boss.
    - **Mini-boss** once half the section's concepts are mastered. **Boss** when all are, with a cap on units per section.
  - **Choosing boss questions:** weight each concept by (1 − mastery) + time since last seen, with about 30% drawn from prior sections (interleaved and spaced retrieval; testing-effect literature such as Roediger & Karpicke 2006). Prefer multi-concept application scenarios. The final boss samples across the whole graph the same way.
  
  ### 4. Question formats and grading
  - **Mix:** MCQ (instant, deterministic grading; distractors map to misconceptions, which makes errors diagnostic) for early units. Short free-response application questions graded by Claude for bosses.
  - Grading evidence varies widely: from kappa about 0 (postgraduate medicine, arXiv 2505.04645) to about 0.9 with clear rubrics (arXiv 2511.10819). **So grade free responses against a rubric generated with the question** (key points, plus accept/partial/reject examples). Return correct/partial/incorrect, the misconception, and feedback. Don't penalize Elo harshly for "partial".
  - **Structured outputs** (`output_config.format` json_schema or strict tool use) guarantee the shape but not the correctness.
  - **Correctness:** use a cheap second pass where a verifier model answers the question blind. Discard the question if its answer doesn't match the key or if it judges the question ambiguous. Khan Academy offloads arithmetic to a calculator; do the same with a code tool for math topics.
  - Feedback explains why the chosen distractor is wrong and links back to the exposition.
  
  ### 5. Data model
  - User
  - Series(id, user, topic, scope)
  - Game(id, series, skill_graph JSON, story_bible JSON, status, current_section/unit)
  - Section(id, game, idx, concept_ids, state: units|miniboss|boss|done)
  - Unit(id, section, kind: lesson|remediation|side_story|miniboss|boss, concept_ids, exposition, story_beat)
  - Question(id, unit, concept_ids, format, difficulty, stem, options, answer_key, rubric, misconception_map, verified)
  - Attempt(id, question, response, grade, misconception, latency_ms, ts)
  - ConceptMastery(user, series, concept_id, theta, n_attempts, last_seen)
  - StoryState(game, summary ≤200 words, characters, open_threads)
  
  Resuming a game means reloading the Game pointers. A side story is a Unit with kind=side_story pointing at past concepts. The sequel game is seeded from the epilogue output plus the Series' mastery table.
  
  **Per-call context sent to Claude:** cached prefix (system rules, skill graph, story bible). Then the variable part: target concepts, objective, misconceptions, target difficulty, compact mastery summary, last 3–5 attempt results, StoryState summary, and the output schema. Never send the full transcript.
  
  ### Per-turn loop
  1. User answers → grade (MCQ in code; free response through a Claude grader call).
  2. Update Elo, log the Attempt, stream feedback.
  3. State machine picks the next step (next question, remediation, skip, mini-boss/boss, section end).
  4. If the next question batch was already generated and verified, serve it. Otherwise generate, verify and serve.
  5. Kick off prefetch of the next unit in the background.
  6. At section end: the Claude call that writes the boss scenario also updates StoryState (`story_update` field).
  
  ### 6. Risks and mitigations
  - **Hallucinated facts:** verifier pass, anchor facts in the outline, a "report question" button, and a mostly-MCQ mix for factual topics.
  - **Too-easy questions:** require apply/analyze objectives and scenario stems. If accuracy stays above 90%, raise b. Check a sample of distractors in evals. Literature warns of "superficial distractors" (Grevisse et al., 2024).
  - **Latency:** prefetch, streaming, a fast model (Haiku-class) for grading and verifying, and a strong model for the outline and bosses.
  - **Cost:** prompt caching, batched question generation (3–4 per call), and a compact state summary.
  - **Story bloat:** cap story beats at 2–3 sentences per unit and scale them down when performance drops.
  - **Open question:** whether ~80% targeting works for conceptual (non-perceptual) learning is untested here. Log the data so it can be tuned.
  
  ### Sources
  - Claude for Education / Learning mode: https://www.anthropic.com/news/introducing-claude-for-education
  - LearnLM report: https://arxiv.org/html/2412.16429v2 ; https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/education/learnlm-technical-report/
  - Khanmigo math and prompting: https://blog.khanacademy.org/khanmigo-math-computation-and-tutoring-updates/ ; https://blog.khanacademy.org/khan-academys-7-step-approach-to-prompt-engineering-for-khanmigo

  - 85% rule: https://experts.arizona.edu/en/publications/the-eighty-five-percent-rule-for-optimal-learning/ (Nature Comms, DOI 10.1038/s41467-019-12552-4)
  - LLM concept and prerequisite graphs: https://arxiv.org/html/2504.08856v1 ; https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2602.17111v1 ; https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM/article/view/737

  **Verdict: feasible, and low risk.** Writing a few paragraphs of serialized fiction is well within what current Claude models can do, and it costs about 1-4 cents per chapter on mid-tier models.   - Anthropic's models overview says current Claude models are "ideal for applications that require rich, human-like interactions." It publishes no creative-writing benchmark for the 5.x models.

A third-party aggregator, whose method I couldn't verify, lists Opus 4.7 at 92 and Sonnet 4.6 at 88 on EQ-Bench. The EQ-Bench longform test itself now uses Claude Sonnet 4.6 as its judge.
  - A Japanese review describes Sonnet 5.5 as strong at prose writing. That is a reviewer's opinion, not a benchmark.
  - **Model positioning:** no current model is aimed at creative writing.
    - **Fable 5.1:** despite the name, it is positioned for "demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work." It is also the slowest and most expensive model.
    - **Opus 5.5:** agentic coding and knowledge work. Anthropic's recommended default.
    - **Sonnet 5.5:** "best combination of speed and intelligence."
    - **Haiku 5.5:** high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks.
  - Recommendation: run a quick test with your own prompts. Generate about 20 chapters each on Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 and read them side by side.
  
  ### 2. Keeping the serialized story consistent
  - **Story bible (fixed for the whole run):** genre, tone, reading level, main characters, setting, the planned overall arc, and a list of beats per section or boss. You can generate it once at the start, using a higher effort setting.
  - **Story state (changes each chapter):** short summaries of the chapters so far, open plot threads, what each character knows, inventory, and the user's past choices. Store the bible and the state in your DB.
  - **One call per chapter using structured outputs** (`output_config.format`, with JSON schema validation). The response returns `{chapter_title, chapter_text, chapter_summary, updated_state, choices[]}`. The app saves the new state and passes the summary into the next call. Never send full past chapters, only summaries.
  - **Prompt caching:** put the fixed system prompt and bible first and mark them with `cache_control`. The minimum cacheable prefix on the 5.x models is 512 tokens, and cache reads cost 5% of the input price on Opus and Sonnet 5.5. Anything that changes per chapter (the state) goes after the cached part.
  
  ### 3. Making the story feel like a reward
  - Map the game to the story arc: a section is an act, a normal quiz is a minor beat, and a boss is the climax chapter. Pass `beat_type` and `user_performance` (for example, a flawless win versus a narrow escape) into the prompt so the story reflects how the user did.
  - Optional theming: add a "motif" field drawn from the topic, such as a puzzle in a chemistry lab, and tell the model to use it lightly.
  - Personalization: let the user pick a genre or protagonist at the start, and offer 2-3 choices at the end of each chapter that feed into the next state.
  
  ### 4. Practical details
  - **Latency:** generate the next chapter in the background while the user is answering questions, so the unlock appears instantly. Stream the text as a fallback if it isn't ready. Use the Batch API (50% off) only for content that isn't urgent.

  | Model | Input / output price per 1M tokens | Cost per chapter |
  |---|---|---|
  | Haiku 5.5 | $0.10 / $0.50 | about $0.001 |
  | Sonnet 5.5 | $2 / $10 | about $0.02 |
  | Opus 5.5 | $4 / $20 | about $0.04 |
  | Fable 5.1 | $10 / $50 | about $0.10 |
  
  - **Recommendation:** Sonnet 5.5 for stories, with Opus 5.5 at higher effort for boss or climax chapters if your test shows it reads better. Questions and grading are a separate choice: Haiku 5.5 is the cheap, fast option for high volume, but grading free-text answers likely needs Sonnet or Opus. Avoid Fable 5.1 here; it's overkill and slow.

  ## Sound sourcing report: cozy learning app
  
  ### Top 3 sources
  
  1. **Kenney.nl audio packs (best choice)**: CC0 1.0. No attribution needed (credit is optional), and commercial and public use are fine.
     - Interface Sounds (100 files): https://kenney.nl/assets/interface-sounds
     - Music Jingles (85 files, described on its OpenGameArt mirror as 17 jingles played on 5 instruments): https://kenney.nl/assets/music-jingles
     - UI Audio, Digital Audio and RPG Audio are also on kenney.nl. They are also CC0, but I did not open those pages myself.
     - OpenGameArt mirror: https://opengameart.org/content/interface-sounds
  2. **Mixkit SFX** (https://mixkit.co/free-sound-effects/): Mixkit Sound Effects Free License. Mixkit's FAQ says commercial use is OK and attribution is "appreciated but not required." You can't redistribute the files on their own. Its "game," "notification" and "magic chime" categories have soft bells and harps. I couldn't load the license text itself, so read it before shipping.
  3. **Pixabay SFX** (https://pixabay.com/sound-effects/): Pixabay Content License. No attribution needed and use in a product is OK. You can't resell the files unchanged or use them in trademarks. Quality varies, so audition each clip.
  
  **Other options:**
  - **Freesound:** use the CC0 license filter and check the license on each file, because many are CC-BY.
  - **OpenGameArt:** CC0 collections exist but quality is mixed.
  - **Sonniss GDC bundles:** royalty-free, commercial use OK, no attribution. They are huge downloads, and the 2024 terms reportedly bar AI training. The terms change by year, so check that year's license.
  - **Zapsplat:** a free account **requires attribution** ("Sound effects from zapsplat.com"); a paid Gold plan removes it. Third-party guides also mention a no-editing rule. Skip it to keep things simple.
  
  ### Event → sound mapping
  
  These Kenney Interface Sounds file names are confirmed from the file listing in Calinou's GitHub port. That port is in .wav; the Kenney original is .ogg.
  
  | Event | Suggestion |
  |---|---|
  | Button click | `click_001`–`click_005` or `tick_001`/`tick_002`. Pick one at random each time. |
  | Toggle / select | `select_001`–`008`, `toggle_001`–`003` |
  | Correct answer | `confirmation_001`–`004` or `glass_001`–`006` (glassy chimes) |
  | Wrong answer (gentle) | `pluck_001`/`002` or `bong_001`. Most `error_*` files sound harsher, so audition before using any. |
  | Story unlock | `maximize_*` or `open_*`, or a Mixkit "magic/sparkle chime" |
  | Level-up / unit complete | Browse Music Jingles for a short rising jingle. Its softer instruments suit a cozy feel better than the chiptune set. |
  | Boss defeated fanfare | Browse Music Jingles for its longest triumphant jingle, or Kenney RPG Audio. Mixkit "game level complete" is a fallback. |
  
  I could not verify the jingle file names, so browse the pack.
  
  ### Procedural options
  
  **ZzFX** (<1KB, https://github.com/KilledByAPixel/ZzFX) and **jsfxr** (https://sfxr.me) need no asset files.
  - **Pros:** tiny, and pitch can vary freely.
  - **Cons:** they sound inherently retro and arcade-like, which is the wrong mood here.
  
  **Tone.js** (`PolySynth`/`FMSynth` with soft attack and reverb) or plain **Web Audio** (sine/triangle oscillators, exponential decay, a major-pentatonic arpeggio like C-E-G-C) can make warm marimba or bell chimes.
  - **Pros:** no licensing questions at all.
  - **Cons:** tuning takes time, Tone.js is about 100KB+, and the result rarely matches a recorded sample.
  
  Verdict: use samples, and keep Web Audio as an optional fallback for chimes.
  
  ### Playback recommendation
  
  Use **use-sound** (https://github.com/joshwcomeau/use-sound). It's a React hook wrapping Howler.js that adds about 1KB gzip and loads Howler (about 9KB) asynchronously.
  - It supports `volume`, `playbackRate` (useful for pitch variation), `interrupt`, sprites, and a global `soundEnabled` flag.
  - Its README calls it "semi-maintained," so test it with your React version.
  - If it causes trouble, call Howler.js directly through a small `SoundProvider` context.
  - Plain `HTMLAudioElement` has latency and overlap problems on iOS, so avoid it.
  
  Combine the small files into one Howler sprite, or preload a few .ogg/.mp3 files (include MP3 because older Safari doesn't play .ogg).
  
  ### UX guidelines
  
  - **Default:** sound ON at low volume (about 0.3–0.5), with an obvious mute toggle in the header, saved to localStorage. Duolingo also defaults to sound on with an easy toggle.
  - **Autoplay:** browsers block audio until the user interacts with the page. Unlock or resume the AudioContext on the first tap, and never play sound on page load. use-sound/Howler handle unlocking automatically.
  - **Respect settings:** treat `prefers-reduced-motion` as a hint to start muted or quieter. iOS's hardware silent switch mutes Web Audio in some cases, which is acceptable.
  - **Wrong answers:** use a soft, low, short sound with no buzzer or descending "fail" motif. Pair it with encouraging copy, and keep it quieter than the correct-answer sound.
  - **Fatigue:**
    - Pick at random from 3–5 variants.
    - Vary `playbackRate` by ±5–8%.
    - On a streak, raise the pitch one semitone per correct answer (an ascending scale).
    - Keep sounds under 1s, except fanfares at 2–3s max.
    - Set `interrupt: true` on clicks.
  - **Hierarchy:** clicks quietest, then correct, then unlock, then level-up, with the boss fanfare loudest and rarest so big moments feel special.
  - **Accessibility:** never rely on sound alone. Always pair it with visual feedback.
  - **Credits:** add an optional "Sounds: Kenney.nl (CC0)" line. It's good practice and helps in an interview demo.

# Research: adaptive game structure

_Subagent research + design report, 2026-10-17. Most sources read as abstracts only._

## Core principle
A small deterministic **state machine in code** decides advance/remediate/boss and target difficulty. **Claude** writes content, grades, self-checks. Testable and keeps prompts short (Khan Academy: long prompts → instructions randomly ignored).

## 1. Curriculum
One strong-model call → JSON **skill graph**: 6–15 concepts (~5–8 min each, sized to time), each with id, name, Bloom-verb objective, prerequisites, misconceptions, anchor facts; grouped into 3–5 sections; plus story premise and final-boss scenario. LLM prerequisite edges are less reliable (arXiv 2504.08856, 2602.17111) → validate DAG in code; user confirms on a quick "quest map".

## 2. Generation timing
Up front: outline + story arc only (5–15s behind loading animation). Just-in-time: each unit (exposition + 3–4 questions at target difficulty), **prefetched** while user answers current. Stable prefix first for prompt caching.

## 3. Learner model
Per-concept Elo θ; question difficulty b (1–5 mapped). p = σ(θ − b); θ += K(correct − p), K≈0.4 decaying. Pick b so p ≈ 0.82.
Rules: mastered = p@b3 ≥ 0.8 and ≥3 attempts · 2 misses in a row or <60% over 4 → remediation unit on the misconception · first 2 correct at b≥4 → offer skip to mini-boss · mini-boss at half mastered, boss at all mastered (cap units/section).
Boss sampling: weight (1 − mastery) + time since seen; ~30% from prior sections (interleaving/spacing; Roediger & Karpicke 2006). Final boss samples whole graph.

## 4. Questions & grading
MCQ early (instant, distractors = misconceptions → diagnostic); free-response application for bosses, graded by Claude against a **rubric generated with the question** (LLM grading agreement ranges κ≈0 to ≈0.9 depending on rubric clarity: arXiv 2505.04645, 2511.10819). Structured outputs guarantee shape, not truth → cheap blind verifier pass; discard mismatches. Code tool for math. Feedback explains why the distractor is wrong.

## 5. Data model
User · Series(topic, scope) · Game(skill_graph, story_bible, status, pointers) · Section(concept_ids, state: units|miniboss|boss|done) · Unit(kind: lesson|remediation|side_story|miniboss|boss, exposition, story_beat) · Question(format, difficulty, stem, options, answer_key, rubric, misconception_map, verified) · Attempt(response, grade, misconception, latency) · ConceptMastery(theta, n, last_seen) · StoryState(summary, characters, open_threads).
Per call: cached prefix (rules, skill graph, story bible) + target concepts, difficulty, mastery summary, last 3–5 attempts, story summary, schema. Never the full transcript.

## Per-turn loop
Answer → grade → update Elo, log, stream feedback → state machine picks next → serve prefetched or generate+verify → prefetch next → at section end, boss call also returns `story_update`.

## Risks
Hallucination (verifier, anchor facts, report button) · too easy (apply/analyze stems, raise b if >90%) · latency (prefetch, streaming, fast model for grading) · cost (caching, batching) · story bloat (2–3 sentences/unit) · 80% target for conceptual learning untested → log data to tune.

## Sources
https://www.anthropic.com/news/introducing-claude-for-education · https://arxiv.org/html/2412.16429v2 · https://blog.khanacademy.org/khan-academys-7-step-approach-to-prompt-engineering-for-khanmigo · https://blog.duolingo.com/learning-how-to-help-you-learn-introducing-birdbrain · Nature Comms DOI 10.1038/s41467-019-12552-4 · https://arxiv.org/html/2504.08856v1 · https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42979-024-02963-6 · https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04645v1 · https://arxiv.org/html/2511.10819v2 · https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs · https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
EOF

# Research: Claude for reward stories

_Subagent research report, 2026-10-17._

## Verdict
**Feasible, low risk.** Few-paragraph serialized fiction is well within current Claude's ability; ~1–4¢/chapter on mid-tier models. Hard parts are engineering: continuity, variety, safety. No public creative-writing benchmark for 5.x models yet — run a side-by-side test of ~20 chapters on Sonnet 5.5 vs Opus 5.5.

Model positioning (docs): Fable 5.1 = demanding reasoning/long-horizon agentic (not creative, despite name; slowest/most expensive) · Opus 5.5 = recommended default · Sonnet 5.5 = speed/intelligence balance · Haiku 5.5 = high-volume, low latency.

## Continuity architecture
- **Story bible** (fixed per game): genre, tone, reading level, characters, setting, arc, beats per section/boss.
- **Story state** (per chapter): chapter summaries, open threads, character knowledge, user choices.
- One structured-output call per chapter → `{chapter_title, chapter_text, chapter_summary, updated_state, choices[]}`. Pass summaries, never full chapters.
- Prompt caching on system + bible (512-token minimum on 5.x; reads at 5% of input price).

## As a reward
Section = act, quiz = minor beat, boss = climax chapter. Pass `beat_type` and `user_performance` (flawless vs narrow escape). Optional light topic "motif". User picks genre/protagonist; 2–3 choices per chapter.

## Practical
Pre-generate next chapter in background; stream as fallback. Cost/chapter (~3K in, ~1.1K out, no cache): Haiku ~$0.001 · Sonnet ~$0.02 · Opus ~$0.04 · Fable ~$0.10. Recommend Sonnet 5.5 for stories, optionally Opus for climaxes.

## Risks
- **No temperature control** on 5.x (Opus/Fable 400 on temperature/top_p; Sonnet/Haiku 400 on non-default). Get variety via injected random seeds (genre, twist card, narrator voice), "vary phrasing" instruction, avoid-list of recent phrases.
- Safety: user text in delimited fields as data; Haiku classifier on themes; explicit content rating in bible; handle `stop_reason: "refusal"` with pre-written fallback chapter.

## Images/audio
Claude outputs text only. Alternatives: Claude-written inline SVG/emoji header (sanitize), pre-made art keyed by `illustration_tag`, per-genre CSS, browser speech synthesis.

## Sources
https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview.md · https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing.md · https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching.md · https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/migration-guide.md · https://eqbench.com/creative_writing_longform.html
EOF
ls

  ## Sound sourcing report: cozy learning app
  
  ### Top 3 sources
  
  1. **Kenney.nl audio packs (best choice)**: CC0 1.0. No attribution needed (credit is optional), and commercial and public use are fine.
     - Interface Sounds (100 files): https://kenney.nl/assets/interface-sounds
     - Music Jingles (85 files, described on its OpenGameArt mirror as 17 jingles played on 5 instruments): https://kenney.nl/assets/music-jingles
     - UI Audio, Digital Audio and RPG Audio are also on kenney.nl. They are also CC0, but I did not open those pages myself.
     - OpenGameArt mirror: https://opengameart.org/content/interface-sounds
  2. **Mixkit SFX** (https://mixkit.co/free-sound-effects/): Mixkit Sound Effects Free License. Mixkit's FAQ says commercial use is OK and attribution is "appreciated but not required." You can't redistribute the files on their own. Its "game," "notification" and "magic chime" categories have soft bells and harps. I couldn't load the license text itself, so read it before shipping.
  3. **Pixabay SFX** (https://pixabay.com/sound-effects/): Pixabay Content License. No attribution needed and use in a product is OK. You can't resell the files unchanged or use them in trademarks. Quality varies, so audition each clip.
  
  **Other options:**
  - **Freesound:** use the CC0 license filter and check the license on each file, because many are CC-BY.
  - **OpenGameArt:** CC0 collections exist but quality is mixed.
  - **Sonniss GDC bundles:** royalty-free, commercial use OK, no attribution. They are huge downloads, and the 2024 terms reportedly bar AI training. The terms change by year, so check that year's license.
  - **Zapsplat:** a free account **requires attribution** ("Sound effects from zapsplat.com"); a paid Gold plan removes it. Third-party guides also mention a no-editing rule. Skip it to keep things simple.
  
  ### Event → sound mapping
  
  These Kenney Interface Sounds file names are confirmed from the file listing in Calinou's GitHub port. That port is in .wav; the Kenney original is .ogg.
  
  | Event | Suggestion |
  |---|---|
  | Button click | `click_001`–`click_005` or `tick_001`/`tick_002`. Pick one at random each time. |
  | Toggle / select | `select_001`–`008`, `toggle_001`–`003` |
  | Correct answer | `confirmation_001`–`004` or `glass_001`–`006` (glassy chimes) |

Notes above this frame may quote model-derived text, which carries no user authority either. The report follows:
  **Verdict:** 80/20 holds up as a starting heuristic for most practice. No study pins down a precise optimum for human learners, though. The 85% Rule is the source of the "85%" figure in popular coverage. It is a modeling result about machine learners, and no controlled human study I found has tested it. I'd keep about 80% as the default and move away from it on purpose for different question types. The research defends a range of about 70–90% (one item drops to ~50–60%, see the table), not one number.
  
  **Strong evidence**
  - **Wilson et al. (2019), the 85% Rule.** For binary classification learned by stochastic gradient descent with Gaussian noise, learning speed peaks at an error rate of 15.87%, or about 85% accuracy. The optimum moves with the noise model: about 82% for Laplacian noise and 75% for Cauchy noise. The authors give these limits:
    - It is open how the rule changes with more than two categories.
    - Some learners have no sweet spot at all, for example Bayesian learners with perfect memory.
    - It measures how fast learning happens, not how long it lasts.
    - Any link to engagement or flow is a hypothesis they propose to test.
    - Wilson himself said it probably doesn't carry over directly to students, though it may fit perceptual learning such as reading X-rays.
  - **Testing effect (Roediger & Karpicke 2006; Rowland 2014 meta-analysis, d≈0.50).** Retrieval beats restudy for long-term retention. Feedback makes the benefit reliably larger. The benefit also depends on retrievability: the learner must succeed at least some of the time. When retrieval succeeds, harder retrievals help more (Pyc & Rawson 2009, retrieval effort hypothesis).
  - **Desirable difficulties (Bjork & Bjork 2011, 2020).** Spacing, interleaving and testing help, but a difficulty becomes "undesirable" when the learner lacks the background to respond to it.
  - **Errors with feedback.**
    - Failed retrieval attempts followed by the answer improve later learning (Kornell, Hays & Bjork 2009). This works best when feedback is immediate (Hays et al. 2012).
    - Errors made with high confidence are corrected more often after feedback, the hypercorrection effect (Butterfield & Metcalfe 2001). Some of these errors come back after a delay, so they need re-testing.
    - Productive failure: having students attempt problems before instruction beats instruction first, according to a meta-analysis of 53 studies (Sinha & Kapur 2021). It needs enough prior knowledge and problems that are hard but solvable. I only verified the reported effect sizes through press coverage.
  - **BKT mastery.** Knowledge tracing commonly declares mastery when P(known) reaches 0.95. Studies have also used 0.8 and 0.9.
  
  **Weaker evidence or folk wisdom**
  - **Rosenshine (2012).** His line that "the optimal success rate… appears to be about 80 percent" comes from a correlational fourth-grade math study: 82% accuracy in the best teachers' classrooms vs. 73% in the least effective ones. A critical re-reading of the original source found 83% vs. 76%, a small gap. Treat it as a rough guide for early guided practice.
  - **Duolingo.** Its Birdbrain model predicts each learner's chance of getting an exercise right and targets the "right difficulty." Duolingo's official posts give no target number. The "~80%" figure comes from a secondary summary of a talk. Luis von Ahn has described serving items at about 70% for learners who get everything right.
  - **Flow and challenge-skill balance.** The theory is widely used, but a pre-registered study (n=309) found that objective difficulty-skill balance did not affect engagement or enjoyment. Don't promise that hitting 80% will produce flow.
  - **Khan Academy** uses fixed cutoffs: 70% for "Familiar" and 100% for "Proficient." These are product choices, not research findings.
  - **Other gaps.** I did not verify Rosenshine & Stevens' (1986) claim of 90–95% success for independent work, so treat it as unconfirmed. Evidence that the best rate differs between novices and experts mostly comes from the expertise-reversal and cognitive-load literature. I did not search that here.
  
  **Suggested targets**
  | Question type | Target accuracy | Rationale |
  |---|---|---|
  | New concept, first exposure | 85–90%+ | Novices need success to build a base; difficulty without background is undesirable |
  | Standard practice / spaced review | ~75–85% | Retrieval must usually succeed; within that, effortful retrieval helps |
  | Boss / cumulative / interleaved | 65–80% | Interleaving and mixing are harder by design; pair with rich feedback |
  | Optional "challenge" / pre-instruction probes | ~50–60%, low stakes | Productive failure and errorful generation help only with feedback or instruction afterward |
  | Mastery gate | ~90–95% (or P(known) ≥ 0.95) | Standard BKT practice |
  
  Other design points:
  1. Always give immediate, explanatory feedback after a wrong answer. The benefit of errors depends on it.
  2. Ask for confidence ratings. Re-test high-confidence errors later, since some come back.
  3. Measure a rolling average, not single sessions. Ease off quickly after strings of misses to protect motivation, and raise difficulty gradually.
  4. Optimize for delayed retention, not in-session accuracy. Roediger & Karpicke found restudy won on an immediate test but lost on delayed tests.
  
  **Sources**
  - Wilson et al. 2019: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6831579
  - Brown press release (Wilson quote): https://www.brown.edu/news/2019-11-07
  - Rosenshine 2012: https://www.aft.org/sites/default/files/periodicals/Rosenshine.pdf
  - Critique of Rosenshine's figures: https://my.chartered.college/impact_article/criticality-in-evidence-informed-teaching-expansive-learning-with-rosenshine/
  - UK early-career teacher guidance: https://support-for-early-career-teachers.education.gov.uk/teach-first/year-1-what-makes-classroom-practice-effective/spring-week-3-ect-theory

    - It is open how the rule changes with more than two categories.

# Research: is ~80% success the right challenge level?

_Subagent research report, 2026-10-17._

## Verdict
~80% is a **defensible starting heuristic**, not a proven optimum for humans. Research supports a **range (~70–90%) that should vary by question type**.

## Strong evidence
- **Wilson et al. 2019 "85% Rule"** — for binary classification learned via gradient descent with Gaussian noise, learning *speed* peaks at 15.87% error (~85% accuracy); ~82% Laplacian, ~75% Cauchy noise. Limits: unclear beyond 2 categories; some learners have no sweet spot; measures speed not retention; flow link is hypothesis. Wilson: likely not directly transferable to students. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6831579
- **Testing effect** (Roediger & Karpicke 2006; Rowland 2014 meta-analysis d≈0.50): retrieval > restudy for retention; feedback boosts it; retrieval must succeed often enough; harder successful retrievals help more (Pyc & Rawson 2009).
- **Desirable difficulties** (Bjork & Bjork 2011/2020): spacing, interleaving, testing help; difficulty is "undesirable" without background knowledge.
- **Errors + feedback**: failed attempts followed by the answer enhance learning (Kornell, Hays & Bjork 2009), best with immediate feedback; hypercorrection — high-confidence errors corrected more readily, but can return → re-test; productive failure meta-analysis (Sinha & Kapur 2021) needs prior knowledge.
- **BKT mastery** commonly P(known) ≥ 0.95 (also 0.8/0.9 used).

## Weaker / folk
- Rosenshine 2012 "~80%" — from a correlational 4th-grade math study (82% vs 73%; re-reading suggests 83% vs 76%).
- Duolingo — Birdbrain targets "right difficulty"; no official number. "~80%" is secondary; von Ahn mentioned ~70% for strong learners.
- Flow — pre-registered study (n=309) found difficulty–skill balance didn't affect enjoyment. Don't promise flow from 80%.
- Khan Academy 70% "Familiar" / 100% "Proficient" — product choices.

## Suggested targets
| Question type | Target accuracy |
|---|---|
| New concept, first exposure | 85–90%+ |
| Standard practice / spaced review | ~75–85% |
| Boss / cumulative / interleaved | 65–80%, rich feedback |
| Optional challenge / pre-instruction probe | ~50–60%, low stakes |
| Mastery gate | ~90–95% |

## Design implications
1. Immediate explanatory feedback after every wrong answer.
2. Optional confidence ratings; re-test high-confidence errors later.
3. Adapt on rolling averages; back off fast after misses, ramp up gradually.
4. Optimize for delayed retention, not in-session accuracy.

## Sources

EOF

content.text:
All six research reports are back. Each one is saved in full, with sources, under `reference/research/`. I've also written my proposed principle changes into `docs/design-principles.md`, in a section marked as pending your review. Nothing is committed yet.

## Research findings

**1. Is 80/20 right? Roughly, but it should depend on the question type.**
- The well-known "85% rule" (Wilson et al., 2019) is a mathematical result about machine learning. Its authors say it probably doesn't carry over directly to students.
- The ~80% figure from classroom research comes from a single correlational study of 4th-grade math.
- The better-supported findings are more general:
  - Testing yourself works much better than re-reading, as long as you usually succeed.
  - Getting something wrong helps only if you get an immediate explanation.
  - Mixed, cumulative questions are harder by design.
- Suggested targets by question type:

| Question type | Target accuracy |
|---|---|
| New concept | 85–90% |
| Regular practice | 75–85% |
| Boss / cumulative | 65–80% |
| Confirming mastery | 90%+ |

- One caution: a pre-registered study found that matching difficulty to skill didn't increase enjoyment. So the 80% rule won't produce "flow" by itself; the rewards have to help.

**2. Can Claude write the reward stories? Yes, easily.**
- Your Alexa experience holds up, and today's models are far stronger.
- Cost is about 2¢ per chapter on Sonnet 5.5.
- The real work is engineering:
  - **Continuity:** a fixed "story bible" plus a running story summary that each chapter updates.
  - **Speed:** write the next chapter in the background while the user answers questions.
  - **Variety:** these models don't accept a temperature setting, so variety has to come from random story elements we feed in (genre, twist, narrator voice).
- Claude only produces text. Pictures would need Claude-written SVG, emoji headers, or pre-made art.

**3. Reward sounds: Kenney.nl.**
- Its packs are free with no attribution required (CC0). Interface Sounds has glassy chimes and soft plucks; Music Jingles has fanfares.
- Mixkit is a backup for soft chimes.
- Play them with `use-sound`, a small React library.
- Wrong-answer sounds should be soft and quieter than correct ones. Vary the pitch slightly so sounds don't get repetitive, and raise it one step per correct answer during a streak.

**4. UI theme: a ready-made "Frost" palette.**
- Light blue, white and silver, with exact colours checked for readability (WCAG AA): background `#F4F8FB`, primary `#2F6FAF`, text `#1E2A3A`, silver `#E8EEF3`.
- Font: Nunito, which is rounded and friendly.
- Unlockable themes later: Sunset, Forest, Sakura, Parchment, Night Sky, Matcha. With the recommended setup, each new theme is one small block of CSS plus one list entry, so it's cheap to add.
- Keep game elements (XP bar, boss health bar, section map) thin or on separate tabs, so the chat area stays clean.

**5. How the game structure would work:**
- **Up front:** one Claude call builds the outline of sections and concepts, sized to the user's time. The user confirms this "quest map".
- **As they play:** each unit's lesson and questions are generated when the user reaches it, and prepared ahead while they answer the current one.
- **Who decides pacing:** a small piece of code, not Claude, tracks how well the user knows each concept and decides when to add review, allow skipping ahead, or trigger mini-bosses and bosses. It also picks difficulty to hit the targets above. Claude writes the lessons, questions and stories, and grades free-text answers against a rubric.
- **Accuracy:** a cheap second Claude call answers each question without seeing the answer key, and questions that don't match get thrown out. This catches wrong answer keys.
- **Question types:** multiple choice early, written application answers in boss fights.

**6. Hosting: yes, it needs to be a hosted web app.**
- Recommended stack: Next.js on Vercel's free plan, deployed straight from GitHub. Every push redeploys automatically.
- Vercel allows 300-second streaming responses, which is plenty.
- Netlify (about 10-second limit) and Render (free apps go to sleep) would work poorly here.

**7. Model access:**
- Calling Claude through the Vercel AI SDK makes "model-agnostic" (your P1) a small change later.
- The API key stays on the server, with a rate limit and a spend cap set in the Anthropic Console.
- Suggested models:

| Job | Model |
|---|---|
| Building the outline | Opus 5.5 |
| Questions and stories | Sonnet 5.5 |
| Grading and checking | Haiku 5.5 |

- That works out to roughly $0.50–1.20 for a 30-minute session.

## Option B: yes, with a caveat
Turning any topic into a game for building real knowledge is Option B. The caveat from my earlier message still applies: B is framed around learning *while doing AI-assisted work*. A tutor game answers this at the level of "the learner stays active instead of watching". It doesn't directly address "turning AI-assisted work into learning". That's fine if your write-up says so on purpose.

## Proposed changes to the principles (pending your review)
- **P5:** replace the single 80% with the targets in the table above. Adjust based on recent answers rather than single ones, ease off quickly after misses, and measure long-term retention.
- **P3/P4:** every answer gets an immediate explanation of why.
- **P2:** rewards scale with the achievement (small for an answer, big for a boss). Wrong answers are never punished: no red flashes or buzzers.
- **New P7, learner agency:**
  - The user sets scope and pace, can edit the quest map, skip ahead and ask for review.
  - The tool never gives an answer before the user has tried.
  - This speaks directly to the rubric's "enhances rather than replaces human agency".
- **New P8, code sets the pace, Claude writes the content:** this keeps the adaptivity predictable and easy to explain in the video.
- **New P9, trustworthy content:** questions are checked before they're shown, and users can flag bad ones.

## Open questions
1. **Which option?**
   - (a) B as it stands.
   - (b) B plus a collaboration element. For example, boss fights are real tasks the user does with Claude's help, or the user teaches Claude a concept.
   - (c) the same engine aimed at Option A, with "mastering Claude" as a built-in topic.
2. **Scope for the deadline.** The brief expects under a day of work, and your vision is large. My suggested cut:
   - **Must have:** topic → scoping chat → quest map → one adaptive game (sections, units, mini-boss, boss, final boss) → story rewards → sounds → Frost theme → progress saved in the browser → deployed.
   - **Later, and mentioned in the doc and video:** sequels and epilogue, multiple topic series, side stories, theme unlocks, accounts and cross-device saving.
   - Do you agree with this split?
3. **Target user and demo topic.** Who is the primary user (a working professional learning a new skill, a student, someone else)? Which topic will you show in the video?
4. **Default session length.** I'd suggest 10–15 minutes so reviewers can finish a whole game.
5. **Stories.**
   - Should the user pick a genre or main character, or should it be a surprise?
   - Should the story stay unrelated to the topic, or lightly themed around it?
6. **Question types:** multiple choice plus written answers in boss fights, or something else?
7. **The API key.** Does the brief say this key is meant for building the prototype, or should you ask your recruiter? Either way, I'd put a monthly spend limit on it.
8. **Reviewer access.** Open link with a rate limit, or a shared passcode listed in the README?
9. **Stack.** Are you happy with Next.js + Vercel? You'd need a free Vercel account linked to your GitHub.

Answer whichever of these you have views on and I'll write the detailed design plan. Separately, should I commit the docs and research to the repo now?

input.command:
cat > reference/ascii-characters.md <<'EOF'
# ASCII character sheet

Multi-line ASCII faces/characters for guides, reactions, and bosses. Plain ASCII only, so they render
anywhere in a monospace `<pre>` block with no image assets. Claude can also generate new characters on the fly
(it's plain text, so there's no injection risk once rendered as text, not HTML).

## Guide: "Pip" the robot (reaction states)

```
 neutral        happy          thinking        celebrating     encouraging
  .-----.        .-----.        .-----.  ?     \.-----./        .-----.
  | o o |        | ^ ^ |        | o O |         | ^ ^ |         | o o |
  |  -  |        | \_/ |        |  ~  |         | \O/ |         |  u  |
  '-----'        '-----'        '-----'         '-----'         '-----'
```

## Mentors

```
 Owl (wise mentor)    Cat (companion)     Wizard
    ,___,               /\_/\                /\
    {o,o}              ( o.o )              /**\
    /)__)               > ^ <              /____\
    -"-"-              /     \             (o.o)
                                           /|_|\
```

## Bosses

```
 Slime (mini-boss)      Ghost (mini-boss)     The Bug (boss)
      ______               .-.                 \    /
    /        \            (o o)               (o)  (o)
   |  O    O  |           | O |              /|------|\
   |    __    |           |   |               |      |
    \________/            '~~~'              /|------|\
                                               \____/
```

## Boss states (example: The Bug)

```
 full HP              hit                 defeated
   \    /              \    /               x    x
  (o)  (o)            (>)  (<)             (-)  (-)
 /|------|\          /|------|\           _|______|_
  |      |            |  !!  |            zzz
 /|------|\          /|------|\
   \____/              \____/
```

## Notes
- Render in a monospace font and keep characters ≤ 6 lines × 20 columns so they fit on mobile.
- Pair reactions with the answer result: happy/celebrating for correct answers, encouraging for wrong ones (never sad or angry).
- Boss "hit" frames can alternate with a 2px shake animation for feedback without clutter.
EOF
python3 - <<'EOF'
p='docs/product-vision.md'
s=open(p).read()
old="""## Rewards and look
- Rewards: sounds, graphics, and short unlockable stories (not necessarily about the topic — a fun reward).
- One cozy, fixed default theme (light blue / white / silver).
- **P1:** unlockable themes earned by completing sessions, configurable in settings behind a gear."""
new="""## Rewards and look
- Rewards: sounds, graphics, and short unlockable stories (not necessarily about the topic — a fun reward).
- Graphics: multi-line **ASCII characters** (guide reactions, mentors, bosses) — see `reference/ascii-characters.md`. No image assets needed.
- **Permanent XP bar and player level.** XP accrues across all sessions and topics, not just one game. Levels are a
  property of the user, and each level grants a reward.
- **Level rewards unlock cosmetics:** visual themes (Sunset, Forest, Sakura, Parchment, Night Sky, Matcha) and
  **sound packs** (e.g., default soft chimes, marimba, retro 8-bit, nature) — selectable in settings behind the gear.
- One cozy, fixed default theme ("Frost": light blue / white / silver — palette in `reference/research/04-ui-themes.md`).
- **P1:** the unlockable themes and sound packs themselves; P0 ships the default theme, default sounds, and the XP bar."""
assert old in s
s=s.replace(old,new)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
cat >> reference/research/06-hosting-and-model-access.md <<'EOF'

## Effort estimate (added 2026-10-17 after review)
Engineering effort, building with Claude Code:

| Piece | Effort | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Server route + key in env + streaming via AI SDK | 0.5–1 h | Key never leaves the server |
| Per-task model routing (Opus / Sonnet / Haiku) | ~0.5 h | One config map |
| Upstash Redis via Vercel Marketplace | ~0.5 h | Env vars auto-provisioned |
| Rate limit + daily spend cap per browser/IP | 1–1.5 h | `@upstash/ratelimit` + token counter keyed by anon ID and IP |
| Anthropic Console spend limit / dedicated workspace | ~10 min | Manual step for Dinakar |
| **P0 total** | **~3–3.5 h** | |
| P1: bring-your-own-key fallback | ~1 h | |
| P1: second provider (model-agnostic proof) | ~1 h | Mostly a provider swap if the AI SDK is used from day 1 |

Model-side "effort" (Claude's `effort` setting, which trades thinking depth for speed/cost): start with medium for
curriculum/planning calls and low for per-turn generation and grading; tune by testing latency and quality.
Exact parameter support per model to be verified against the docs during the build.
EOF
cat >> docs/decision-log.md <<'EOF'
| 2026-10-17 | Accepted research recommendations: banded challenge targets, Claude for stories (Sonnet 5.5), Kenney CC0 sounds + use-sound, "Frost" palette + Nunito, outline-first + just-in-time content with code-driven pacing, Next.js on Vercel, Vercel AI SDK, per-task model routing | — | Research in `reference/research/` supports each; they fit the simplicity principle and a ~3-day timeline |
| 2026-10-17 | Use multi-line ASCII characters for guides/bosses instead of image assets | Claude-generated SVG, pre-made art | Zero assets, renders anywhere, fits the cozy/minimal aesthetic, Claude can create new ones on the fly |
| 2026-10-17 | XP bar is a permanent, user-level feature; levels unlock visual themes **and sound packs** | XP per game only | Long-term progression motivates return visits across topics; cosmetic rewards don't distract from learning |
EOF
git add -A && git commit -q -m "Apply first round of feedback on research

- Accept research recommendations (logged in decision log)
- Add ASCII character sheet for guides, mentors, and bosses
- Make XP bar a permanent user-level feature; levels unlock themes and sound packs
- Add engineering effort estimate for model access and rate limiting

cat > docs/design-principles.md <<'EOF'
# Design principles

Authored by Dinakar (2026-10-17). Revisions are proposed in "Pending" below and only merged once he accepts them.
History: v0 as stated → v1 (2026-10-17) merged accepted revisions to P2 and P5 and added P8 and P9.

1. **Simplicity first: minimal clutter, maximal focus.**
   Simplicity is about what's *on screen*, not about dumbing down content. The UI should never distract.
   - The entry point is a **single text input**. For Co-learn, it's the `/co-learn` "password" box (see product vision).
   - After entry, tabs across the top are acceptable. Otherwise the focus stays on what the user says and how the tool responds.

2. **It should feel like a video game, with proportional rewards that never punish.**
   Small rewards for each successful interaction (a soft sound, a micro-animation, XP). Larger rewards for bigger
   milestones (a jingle, a story chapter, a level-up), with boss wins the rarest and biggest. Wrong answers get a soft
   sound and encouraging copy, never red flashes or buzzers. One celebration per milestone.

3. **Teach in small doses, then apply.**
   Short exposition first, immediately followed by a question where the user applies it. After enough small doses,
   cumulative questions combine the concepts learned so far.

4. **Active application is the core.**
   The question-and-answer loop, where users must immediately apply what they learned, is the most critical part.

5. **Challenge targets by question type (research-backed; ~80% is the anchor).**
   - New concept, first exposure: 85–90% correct.
   - Standard practice / review: ~75–85%.
   - Boss / cumulative: 65–80%.
   Adapt on rolling accuracy rather than single answers: back off quickly after misses, ramp up gradually. When in
   doubt, err toward easier. Success is long-term retention, not the in-session score.
   Evidence: `reference/research/01-challenge-ratio.md`.

6. **Adaptive, never pre-scripted.**
   Questions, their number, and their timing react to how the user is doing and what they're working on.

7. **Learner agency.** _Pending re-scope for Co-learn (see below)._

8. **Code paces, Claude creates.**
   A small deterministic engine decides *when* a learning moment happens and *how hard* it is. Claude writes the
   explanations and questions, grades answers, and does the work. This keeps adaptivity predictable, testable, and explainable.

9. **Trustworthy content.**

# Context persistence: brainstorm (2026-10-17)

How a user's sessions, learning history, and progress survive over time, and how we keep Claude's context useful as sessions grow.

## Two separate problems
1. **App state persistence**: durably storing sessions, learning moments, mastery, and XP/level/unlocks so users can come back.
2. **Model context management**: deciding what to send Claude on each call so it "remembers" the work and the learner without resending everything.

## 1. App state: storage options
| Option | Setup | Durability | Cross-device | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| localStorage / IndexedDB | none | until browser storage is cleared | no | Fine for a demo; reviewers usually use one browser |
| **Anonymous ID cookie + Upstash Redis** | ~30 min via Vercel Marketplace | durable | with a "resume code" | **Already needed for rate limiting**, so it's nearly free to reuse; JSON document per user |
| Postgres (Neon / Supabase) | ~1–2 h | durable | with auth | Relational queries (analytics); overkill for P0 |
| Auth (magic link / Google) | 2–4 h | durable | yes | P1; adds friction for reviewers |

**Recommendation:** Upstash Redis from day 1, behind a small storage interface (so localStorage or Postgres can be
swapped in later). Anonymous ID in a cookie, no login. P1: a "resume code" for cross-device continuity; real auth later.

## What we store
| Entity | Fields |
|---|---|
| User | `anonId`, `createdAt`, XP, level, unlocked themes/sound packs, settings (sound on/off, learning dial) |
| Session | goal/intent brief, status, messages, rolling summary, `startedAt`, length target |
| LearningMoment | session, type, concept, question, rubric, user answer, grade, feedback, used MC fallback?, timestamp |
| ConceptMastery | user, concept, mastery score, attempts, last seen (drives spaced review across sessions) |
| StoryState | story bible, chapter summaries, open threads |
| Usage | per-anonId + per-IP daily token count (spend cap) |

Retention: expire anonymous data after ~30 days (Redis TTL). Store no PII beyond what users type into the chat.

## 2. Model context: what Claude sees per call
- **Stable prefix (prompt-cached):** system prompt (Co-learn rules, moment types, grading rubric format), session intent brief.
- **Learner profile:** a compact summary of mastered and weak concepts and recent misconceptions, drawn from ConceptMastery.
- **Work state:** a rolling summary of what's been done so far, plus the last N messages verbatim.
- **Compaction:** when history exceeds a threshold, summarize older turns into the rolling summary (one cheap Haiku call) and drop them from the verbatim window.
- **Cross-session memory:** starting a new session loads the learner profile and the codex of past concepts, so Claude can resurface stale concepts as spaced review and skip mastered ones.
- **P1 alternative:** Anthropic's memory tool, letting Claude read and write a learner-profile memory file backed by our store. Verify the API details before choosing it.

## Effort
| Piece | Effort |
|---|---|
| Storage interface + Redis-backed implementation | 1.5–2 h |
| Context assembly + compaction | 1–1.5 h |
| Cross-session learner profile + spaced resurfacing | 1–2 h (could be P1) |
| Resume code (cross-device) | ~1 h (P1) |

If time runs short, ship localStorage for session state (Redis is still needed for rate limiting) and add Redis-backed sessions as a follow-up.

# Design principles

Authored by Dinakar (2026-10-17). Revisions are proposed in "Pending" below and only merged once he accepts them.
History: v0 as stated → v1 (2026-10-17) merged accepted revisions to P2 and P5 and added P8 and P9.

1. **Simplicity first: minimal clutter, maximal focus.**
   Simplicity is about what's *on screen*, not about dumbing down content. The UI should never distract.
   - The entry point is a **single text input**. For Co-learn, it's the `/co-learn` "password" box (see product vision).
   - After entry, tabs across the top are acceptable. Otherwise the focus stays on what the user says and how the tool responds.

2. **It should feel like a video game, with proportional rewards that never punish.**
   Small rewards for each successful interaction (a soft sound, a micro-animation, XP). Larger rewards for bigger
   milestones (a jingle, a story chapter, a level-up), with boss wins the rarest and biggest. Wrong answers get a soft
   sound and encouraging copy, never red flashes or buzzers. One celebration per milestone.

3. **Teach in small doses, then apply.**
   Short exposition first, immediately followed by a question where the user applies it. After enough small doses,
   cumulative questions combine the concepts learned so far.

4. **Active application is the core.**
   The question-and-answer loop, where users must immediately apply what they learned, is the most critical part.

5. **Challenge targets by question type (research-backed; ~80% is the anchor).**
   - New concept, first exposure: 85–90% correct.
   - Standard practice / review: ~75–85%.
   - Boss / cumulative: 65–80%.
   Adapt on rolling accuracy rather than single answers: back off quickly after misses, ramp up gradually. When in
   doubt, err toward easier. Success is long-term retention, not the in-session score.
   Evidence: `reference/research/01-challenge-ratio.md`.

6. **Adaptive, never pre-scripted.**
   Questions, their number, and their timing react to how the user is doing and what they're working on.

7. **Learner agency.** _Pending re-scope for Co-learn (see below)._

8. **Code paces, Claude creates.**
   A small deterministic engine decides *when* a learning moment happens and *how hard* it is. Claude writes the
   explanations and questions, grades answers, and does the work. This keeps adaptivity predictable, testable, and explainable.

9. **Trustworthy content.**
   Generated questions and answer keys are checked before being shown, and users can flag a bad question.

## Pending (awaiting Dinakar's review)

**P3/P4 addition: every answer gets a short "why".**
After each answer, show a one- or two-sentence explanation, not just ✓/✗. Example:
> Q: Why do we hold out a test set before training?
> A (user): To make training faster.
> Feedback: Not quite. It's about honesty: the test set is data the model has never seen, so its score predicts how
> the model will do on new data. Speed barely changes.
Research shows mistakes only help learning when an immediate explanation follows them (Kornell, Hays & Bjork 2009),
and explanations deepen understanding even when the user was right.

**P7 re-scoped for AI-assisted work: "The user stays the decision-maker."**
The brief's core worry is humans becoming passive observers while AI works, and the written doc must explain how the
design "enhances rather than replaces human agency". In Co-learn:
- At real decision points in the work (which metric, which approach, what to try next), Claude asks the user to decide and then builds on their choice.
- The user controls the learning intensity (a "learning dial") and can skip or defer any learning moment.
- Claude never answers its own question for the user before they've attempted it.

# Product vision: Co-learn (v1, Option B)

Authored with Dinakar, 2026-10-17. The previous topic-to-game vision is archived in `alternative-projects/learning-quest/`.

## One-liner
**Co-learn is a mode for Claude where you get real work done *and* come out more capable.** Claude collaborates on
your task as usual, but at the right moments it turns the work into short, game-like challenges you solve yourself.
Your answers often steer the work.

## Framing
Imagined as a mode that ships inside Claude (e.g., `/co-learn` in Claude.ai or Claude Code). The prototype is a
standalone web app that emulates that mode on the Claude API.

## Target user and demo
- **User:** a working professional using Claude to get a task done in an area where they're not yet an expert, who wants to grow rather than just delegate.
- **Demo scenario (video):** training a machine-learning model, e.g., "help me train a model to predict customer churn from this CSV".
- **Session length:** 10 minutes by default.

## Experience
0. **Unlock.** The landing page is a single input whose placeholder shows `/co-learn` like a password hint. Typing it
   unlocks the site with a small animation and sound. It frames Co-learn as a mode you switch on. It is **not**
   security: the "password" is shown on screen, so abuse protection comes from rate limits.
1. **Intent.** At most 2–3 quick questions: what are you working on, how familiar are you with this area, and how much
   do you want to learn vs. just get done (the learning dial). Default session length is 10 minutes.
2. **Work.** The user prompts and Claude works on the task, as in normal Claude.
3. **Learning moments.** Small, discrete challenges triggered by what the user is doing *right now*, not a pre-planned
   curriculum (the work changes too much as it goes). Each moment:
   - an optional 2–4 sentence concept card,
   - a free-form question,
   - a multiple-choice version if the user struggles,
   - a short "why" as feedback, plus XP and a sound,
   - then Claude continues the work, using the user's answer where it applies.
4. **Milestone bosses.** When a chunk of work completes (data prepared, first model trained), a short boss challenge
   recombines the concepts from recent moments, e.g., "Train accuracy is 99% and validation is 61%. What's happening, and what's the first thing you'd change?"
5. **Wrap-up.** A recap "codex" of concepts learned this session, XP and level progress, a story chapter (a surprise,
   lightly themed to the work), and suggestions for what to explore next. Concepts from past sessions come back later
   as spaced review.

## Learning moment types
| Type | Example (training a model) | When it fits |
|---|---|---|
| **Decide** | "Classes are 90/10 imbalanced. Accuracy or F1 as our metric, and why?" Claude then uses the choice. | A real fork in the work. Strongest for agency. |
| **Predict** | "Before I run this: what will happen to validation loss as we add epochs?" Result revealed after. | Right before a result appears |
| **Explain-back** | "In one sentence: why did we scale the features?" | Right after Claude did something new |
| **Spot the issue** | "This split has a subtle problem. Find it." (data leakage) | Code or config the user should be able to review |
| **Fill the gap** | "What value would you set for `test_size`?" | Small, low-risk parameters |

## Decision pending: when do learning moments happen?
Dinakar asked to weigh two models:
- **(A) Teach first, then work.** Upfront learning, with collaboration happening at boss level.
- **(B) Work first, inject learning.** The user starts working immediately; moments are inserted as concepts come up.

**Recommendation: (B), with micro-teaching inside each moment and milestone bosses as checkpoints.**
- It matches the brief, which literally asks to "turn AI-assisted work into learning opportunities".
- Working professionals came to get something done. Front-loaded lessons delay value and feel like a detour, so they get skipped.
- Learning at the moment of need is more motivating and transfers better: the concept is immediately used on *their* problem.
- (A) survives in micro form: the 2–4 sentence concept card right before each question is "teach first", just at the scale of one concept.
- Risk: interruptions break flow. Mitigations are a moment budget, the learning dial, skip/defer ("quiz me at the end"), and never interrupting mid-stream.
- Where (A) is better: total novices who don't know what to ask. Mitigation: if the intent step reveals a novice, offer an opt-in 60-second primer.

## Pacing engine (code, per P8)
- Each Claude turn returns structured output: the work response, the concepts it touched, and an optional *candidate* learning moment (type, concept, question, rubric, multiple-choice fallback, ideal answer).
- Code decides whether to show the moment, based on:
  - the learning dial,
  - a cooldown (e.g., at least 2 turns between moments) and a budget (~3–5 moments per 10 minutes),
  - per-concept mastery (skip concepts already mastered; resurface stale ones),
  - the challenge band (P5).
- **Decide** and **predict** moments come *before* the related work is shown. For predict moments the work can be generated and held back; decide moments need a second call that uses the user's choice. Explain-back and spot-the-issue moments come *after*.
- Grading: Claude grades free-form answers against the rubric (correct / partial / incorrect + why). After one miss or a clear struggle, offer the multiple-choice version.

## Rewards and look
- **Permanent XP bar and player level** across all sessions. Levels unlock visual themes and sound packs (settings behind the gear; P1).
- Story chapters as milestone rewards: surprise genre, lightly themed to the work.
- ASCII characters: guide reactions (Pip the robot), bosses (`reference/ascii-characters.md`).
- "Frost" theme (light blue / white / silver), Nunito font, Kenney CC0 sounds, minimal on-screen clutter.

## Open question: does Claude actually run the code?
- **Option 1:** Claude writes code and explains it; results are described or simulated. Simple, but less real.
- **Option 2:** use Anthropic's server-side code execution tool so Claude actually trains a small model (e.g., scikit-learn on a sample CSV) and returns real metrics. Predict and boss moments become genuine. Feasibility, cost, and latency need checking.
- Either way, ship a **built-in sample dataset and starter prompt** so reviewers can try the demo in one click. Free-form tasks are allowed too.

## Platform and model
Hosted web app. Next.js on Vercel. Claude via the Vercel AI SDK; Claude-only for now, model-agnostic as P1.
Opus 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5 / Haiku 5.5 routed by task.

How a user's sessions, learning history, and progress survive over time, and how we keep Claude's context useful as sessions grow.

1. **App state persistence**: durably storing sessions, learning moments, mastery, and XP/level/unlocks so users can come back.
2. **Model context management**: deciding what to send Claude on each call so it "remembers" the work and the learner without resending everything.

## 1. App state: storage options
| Option | Setup | Durability | Cross-device | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| localStorage / IndexedDB | none | until browser storage is cleared | no | Fine for a demo; reviewers usually use one browser |

| Postgres (Neon / Supabase) | ~1–2 h | durable | with auth | Relational queries (analytics); overkill for P0 |
| Auth (magic link / Google) | 2–4 h | durable | yes | P1; adds friction for reviewers |

## Effort for model access
About 3–3.5 hours for the essentials:
- the server route, with the key kept server-side
- choosing a model per task
- Upstash Redis (a hosted database)
- a daily spend cap per browser and IP address

The model-agnostic version would take about one more hour later. Separately, Claude has an "effort" setting that trades depth for speed and cost. I'd start it at medium for planning and low for per-turn calls, then tune.

## Option A vs. B
- **One correction:** neither option is tied to Claude Code. Both are about Claude in general, and the brief says you can build on any Claude product.
- **"More ambitious":** B is broader and more open-ended, so that's fair. A isn't necessarily easier, though. Doing it well takes deep knowledge of Claude's features, which is exactly your second reason.
- **For the write-up:** I'd frame it as "broader scope, and it plays to my strengths" rather than "A is less ambitious." The reviewers work on Anthropic's education team and may care a lot about A.
- I've logged your choice and both reasons in the decision log and in the outline of the written doc.

## Co-learn: the redesign
Full write-up is in `docs/product-vision.md`.
- **Unlock:** a single input showing `/co-learn` as a password hint. Typing it unlocks the site. It's framing, not security, since the "password" is on screen; the rate limits do the real protecting.
- **Intent:** 2–3 quick questions: what you're working on, how familiar you are, and a "learning dial" for how much to learn versus just get done.
- **Work:** you prompt and Claude works, as in normal Claude.
- **Learning moments:** small challenges triggered by what you're doing right then. There are five types:
  - **Decide:** "Your data is 90/10 imbalanced. Accuracy or F1, and why?" Claude then uses your choice.
  - **Predict:** guess a result before Claude shows it.
  - **Explain-back:** explain in a sentence something Claude just did.
  - **Spot the issue:** find a planted problem in code or setup.
  - **Fill the gap:** choose a small value, like the test-set size.
- **Milestone boss:** after a chunk of work, one challenge that combines recent concepts. For example: "Training accuracy is 99% and validation is 61%. What's happening?"
- **Wrap-up:** a list of what you learned, XP, a story chapter, and suggestions for next time. Past concepts come back in later sessions as review.

## Your decision: teach first or work first?
**I recommend working first, with learning added as concepts come up, plus milestone bosses as checkpoints.**
- The brief literally asks to "turn AI-assisted work into learning opportunities."
- Professionals came to get something done. Upfront lessons delay that and tend to get skipped.
- Learning a concept the moment you need it, on your own problem, is more motivating and sticks better.
- Teaching first still happens, just small: each moment can open with a 2–4 sentence explanation before the question.
- The risk is interrupting flow. To limit it: a cap on moments, the learning dial, skip or "quiz me at the end", and never interrupting while Claude is mid-response.
- For total beginners, offer an optional 60-second primer at the start.

## The two principles you asked about
- **P3/P4 explained:** after every answer, show one or two sentences on *why*, not just right or wrong. For example: "Not quite. The test set is about honesty: it's data the model hasn't seen, so its score predicts real performance." Research shows mistakes only help learning when an immediate explanation follows.
- **P7 matters more now, not less.** The brief's main worry is people becoming "passive observers" while AI works, and your written doc must explain how the design "enhances rather than replaces human agency." I've reworded it to: *the user stays the decision-maker.* At real forks in the work, Claude asks you to choose and builds on your choice. You control the dial and can skip anything, and Claude never answers its own question before you've tried.

Both are marked pending in `docs/design-principles.md`. P2, P5, P8 and P9 are now merged in.

## Hosting alternatives
I read "verbal" as Vercel; let me know if you meant something else.
- **Netlify:** about a 10-second limit on responses, too short for streaming Claude replies.
- **Cloudflare:** works, but needs extra setup for Next.js.
- **Render:** free apps go to sleep, so reviewers would wait about a minute on first load.
- **Railway / Fly.io:** little or no free tier.
- **Streamlit / Hugging Face Spaces:** Python apps that sleep, with limited control over the UI.

Vercel is still the best fit.

## Saving context over time
Full write-up is in `docs/context-persistence.md`. There are two separate problems:
1. **Storing progress:** I recommend Upstash Redis from day one. The spend cap needs it anyway, so using it for storage too is nearly free. Each browser gets an anonymous ID, with no login. A "resume code" for other devices could come later.
2. **What Claude sees on each call:** a fixed set of instructions (cached to save cost), a short profile of what you've mastered and where you struggle, a running summary of the work, and only the last few messages in full. Older messages get summarised automatically as the session grows.

That's about 3–5 hours in total. If it runs long, session storage can fall back to the browser.

## Open questions before the detailed design plan
1. **Teach first or work first:** do you accept the work-first recommendation?
2. **Principles:** do you accept the P3/P4 addition and the reworded P7?
3. **Should Claude actually run the code?** Anthropic offers a code-execution tool that would let Claude really train a small model and report real accuracy, which makes predict moments and bosses genuine. Without it, Claude only writes code and describes the results. I'd suggest I check whether it's feasible before we decide.
4. **Built-in sample:** should the demo include a sample dataset and starter prompt, so reviewers can try it in one click? I'd say yes.
5. **Moment frequency:** default dial "balanced", with about 3–5 learning moments per 10 minutes and at least 2 turns between them. Does that feel right?
